newsitem.title: JAPAN: Thailand has no plans to ask for Japan aid - embassy.
newsitem.headline: Thailand has no plans to ask for Japan aid - embassy.

text.p: Thailand's Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya has no plans at the moment to ask Japan for financial assistance to help ease a credit crunch in the country when he visits Tokyo next week, a Thai embassy official in Tokyo said on Thursday.
"He has just become finance minister. He would probably like to introduce himself and get to know Japanese government officials and explain the situation in Thailand," the official said.
"It's not clear and no decision has been made on what's in store at the meetings. But I can say at the moment that it is not for that reason (to seek Japanese financial assistance)," he said.
"We have enough international reserves for at least six months...so I don't see that we have a need at the moment for a (loan) package. It's just speculation," he said.
The Thai government will consider the loans at the right time, he said. "But I don't see this is as the right time yet."
Thanong and Foreign Affairs Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn will be in Tokyo from July 17 to 18 for an unofficial visit.

Embassy officials have said that Thanong will meet with Bank of Japan (BOJ) Governor Yasuo Matsushita and Sakura Bank Ltd officials. He also plans to meet with Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, but the embassy said that a meeting has not yet been fixed.

Thai officials in Bangkok said on Wednesday that the government was studying the possibility of tapping multi-billion-dollar foreign loans to help ease a credit crunch, but so far no borrowing decision had been made.
A senior official of Japan's Ministry of Finance has been in Thailand to negotiate the overall scheme, a Japanese bank official said.

The Nihon Keizai Shimbun business daily said on Thursday that the Japanese government and financial industry will take a leadership role in extending financial aid to Thailand along with other international organisations such as the International Monetary Fund and countries such as the United States and those in Southeast Asia.
The report said the loan package is expected to be over $20 billion, of which Japan may be asked to contribute up to 50 to 60 percent of the total.
Japanese finance ministry officials said that no requests have been made from Thailand and that the ministry could not comment on the reported Thai loan package.
"There has not been a request from Thai authorities for financial cooperation. Therefore, we can't comment on media reports about financial assistance," a Japanese finance ministry official said.
"But we will keep in close contact with Thai authorities and deal appropriately with the situation," he added.
The Thai embassy official in Tokyo said that Thailand was keeping in touch with international organisations such as the IMF and that such contacts were not out of the ordinary.
The embassy official said, however, that the situation was fluid and flexibility was needed, as nothing was certain.

"Japanese businesspeople have told me that they feel this is a temporary situation and that we have strong economic fundamentals to go on. This is just a matter of arranging, adjusting to international flows and markets," he said, adding that there were no threats from Japanese businesses to abandon their investments in Thailand.
